cultivar: Chinary seedling bushes (Camellia sinensis var. sinensis) and Darjeeling clonals such as AV2, B157, P312 and T78
processing: Hard, long wither, gentle orthodox rolling and only partial oxidation (often well under half) before firing; the light oxidation keeps much of the leaf green and the cup pale and bright.
harvest_season: Late February or early March to mid-April, after winter dormancy; the earliest lots after the first spring showers are the most sought-after.
appearance_dry: Wiry, mixed olive-green, brown and silver-tipped leaf that looks more like a green or oolong tea than a black one.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold to light amber, bright and clear.
appearance_wet: Soft, mostly green to olive leaf with brownish edges, slightly uneven in colour.
taste_profile: Fresh, floral and lightly astringent: white flowers, green grape and apricot, a hint of cut grass and a clean, drying finish.

brewing.notes: Water well below the boil (80–90 °C) and no milk; boiling water pulls out harsh tannin and buries the florals. A good lot takes a second, longer steep.

vintage_note: Sold by flush and year: look for 'First Flush' plus the harvest year (2025, 2026…) and the estate name on the pack, often with an invoice (lot) number. Early lots ship from March and the trade peaks in spring; a first flush is at its best within 6–12 months of picking and loses its fresh florals after about a year, so last year's first flush should cost less. Grade codes such as FTGFOP1 appear on labels but say little about quality compared with the garden, the flush and the lot.
description:
Darjeeling first flush is the spring picking from the gardens around Darjeeling in the hills of northern West Bengal, grown between roughly 600 and 2,000 metres. It is the tea that makes people rethink what 'black tea' means: pale, floral and brisk, closer to a green oolong than to anything you would put milk in. Only leaf from the district's registered gardens may legally carry the name, which is protected as a geographical indication in India and the EU.

The bushes sit dormant through the cold, dry winter, so the first shoots after the spring showers are small, slow-grown and concentrated. Makers give that leaf a long, hard wither, roll it gently and oxidise it only partway before firing, which is why the dry leaf looks mottled green, brown and silver and why the cup stays pale gold rather than copper. Technically it is a black tea by process; in the cup it behaves like something in between.

Expect white flowers, green grape, a little apricot and a grassy freshness, with the brisk, lightly drying finish that Darjeeling is known for. The classic mistake is treating it like breakfast tea: boiling water and five minutes gives you harsh tannin and not much else. Brew it like a delicate oolong, water around 85 °C, three minutes, and give a good lot a second, longer steep. No milk.

It is sold by estate, flush and year. Grade codes such as FTGFOP1 ('Finest Tippy Golden Flowery Orange Pekoe, grade 1') describe leaf size and tip, not taste; the garden name, the harvest year and the invoice number tell you much more. Well-known names include Castleton, Margaret's Hope, Jungpana, Makaibari, Glenburn, Goomtee and Puttabong, and clonal lots (usually from the AV2 bush) are the most floral and the most expensive. For years more tea was sold as 'Darjeeling' worldwide than the district could grow, so buy from shops that name the garden and the lot and be wary of cheap blends.

Drink it fresh: a first flush peaks in the months after picking and fades within about a year. If you love the aroma but want more body, the second flush from the same garden is the natural next step.
sources_note: Native name given in Nepali (the language of the Darjeeling hills); Bengali (দার্জিলিং চা) or Hindi (दार्जिलिंग चाय) would also be defensible.
